title: Rigidity of the positive twist under an absolute isomorphism of projective lines
statement: Let $k$ and $l$ be fields [def-weil-field]. Write $P=\mathbf P^1_k$ and $Q=\mathbf P^1_l$, with their line bundles $\mathcal O_P(1)$ and $\mathcal O_Q(1)$ [def-sc-p1-standard, def-sc-invertible-module]. Let $u:P\xrightarrow{\sim}Q$ be an isomorphism of schemes; no identification of $k$ with $l$ is specified. Let $\phi:u^*\mathcal O_Q(1)\to\mathcal O_P(1)$ be an $\mathcal O_P$-linear morphism [def-pc-module-pullback, def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. If the map induced by $\phi$ at the generic point of the integral scheme $P$ is nonzero [def-sc-generic-point, def-pc-integral-scheme], then $\phi$ is an isomorphism of $\mathcal O_P$-modules.

source.place: Tag 0C5R (resolve-lemma-proper-birational-regular-surfaces), conormal degree-1 argument; supported by divisors.tex Tag 0BXJ (divisors-lemma-Pic-projective-space-UFD), n=1, and the standard-chart calculation of sections from def-sc-p1-standard. This formulation permits different residue fields.

proof.text: For any field $K$, apply [lem-sc-p1-twist-sections]. If $d<0$, the equality $p(t)=t^d q(1/t)$ forces $p=q=0$, because the left side has only nonnegative powers and the right side only strictly negative powers. If $d\geq0$, the solutions have basis $(t^j,s^{d-j})$ for $0\leq j\leq d$: comparison of Laurent coefficients writes each solution uniquely as a $K$-linear combination of these pairs. Thus $\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_K,\mathcal O(d))$ has dimension $d+1$ for $d\geq0$ and is zero otherwise. In degree zero the chart bases glue to identify $\mathcal O(0)$ with the structure sheaf [def-sc-p1-standard]; its global functions are exactly the constant pairs $(c,c)$. This identifies $\Gamma(\mathbf P^1_K,\mathcal O)$ with $K$ as rings, since addition and multiplication are componentwise. In degree one there are exactly two basis sections.

source.place: Statement, followed by Laurent-coefficient comparison; standard charts from def-sc-p1-standard.

proof.text: The inverse scheme map to $u$ gives an inverse to its map on global functions, so Step 1 identifies $u^\sharp$ with a field isomorphism $\sigma:l\xrightarrow{\sim}k$. Put $L=u^*\mathcal O_Q(1)$. Explicitly, for an open $U\subseteq P$, the inverse-image colimit has the terminal neighbourhood $u(U)$, since $u$ is a homeomorphism. Hence inverse image has sections $\mathcal O_Q(1)(u(U))$. In [def-pc-module-pullback], the ring map $\mathcal O_Q(u(U))\to\mathcal O_P(U)$ is an isomorphism, so the tensor presheaf has these same sections with scalars transported by this ring isomorphism. The map is $m\mapsto1\otimes m$; its inverse sends $a\otimes m$ to $(u^\sharp_U)^{-1}(a)m$. Their composites send $m$ to $m$ and $a\otimes m$ to $1\otimes (u^\sharp_U)^{-1}(a)m=a\otimes m$, using the tensor balancing relation. They commute with restriction and are inverse on the tensor presheaf. Its identified target is already a sheaf, so sheafification preserves the inverse maps and gives the asserted identification of $L(U)$. In particular they give an additive bijection $T:\Gamma(Q,\mathcal O_Q(1))\to\Gamma(P,L)$ satisfying $T(am)=\sigma(a)T(m)$. A basis of the source maps to a $k$-basis: span follows by applying $T$ to an expansion, and independence follows by writing each coefficient as $\sigma(a)$ and using injectivity of $T$. Consequently $\dim_k\Gamma(P,L)=2$. The same local formula transports each local basis of $\mathcal O_Q(1)$ to a local basis of $L$. On each such open $L$ is the structure sheaf, so it is locally quasi-coherent as well as locally free of rank one, hence invertible [def-sc-invertible-module].

source.place: Tag 0C5R, resolve-lemma-proper-birational-regular-surfaces, conormal degree-1 argument; detailed argument using the standard-chart section formula.

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-projective-line-invertible-classification] over $k$ to the invertible module $L$ from Step 2. Choose an isomorphism $e:L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal O_P(d)$ for the resulting integer $d$. Its map on global sections is $k$-linear and bijective, since $e$ and its inverse are morphisms of $\mathcal O_P$-modules. Steps 1 and 2 give $2=\dim_k\Gamma(P,\mathcal O_P(d))$. Negative $d$ would give zero; for nonnegative $d$ this dimension is $d+1$, forcing $d=1$. We therefore have $e:L\xrightarrow{\sim}\mathcal O_P(1)$.

source.place: Tag 0BXJ, divisors-lemma-Pic-projective-space-UFD, n=1; dimension calculation in Steps 1 and 2.

proof.text: Let $\psi=\phi\circ e^{-1}$, an endomorphism of $\mathcal O_P(1)$. On each standard chart, its generator $g_i$ gives a unique regular function $a_i$ with $\psi(g_i)=a_i g_i$, by linearity [def-weil-sheaf-of-modules-category]. On the overlap $g_0=t^{-1}g_1$ [def-sc-p1-standard], so $a_0t^{-1}g_1=t^{-1}a_1g_1$; cancelling the unit $t^{-1}$ and the basis $g_1$ gives $a_0=a_1$. The sheaf gluing axiom gives a global regular function $a$ restricting to both. Step 1 says $a=c$ for some $c\in k$. Hence $\psi=c\,\mathrm{id}$ on both charts and therefore on $P$.

source.place: Tag 0C5R, resolve-lemma-proper-birational-regular-surfaces, conormal degree-1 argument; detailed argument using the standard-chart section formula.

proof.text: If $c=0$, then $\psi=0$ and $\phi=\psi\circ e=0$, contradicting the assumed nonzero map at the generic point. Thus $c\neq0$. Multiplication by $c^{-1}\in k$ is an inverse of $\psi$, and $e^{-1}\circ(c^{-1}\mathrm{id})$ is an inverse of $\phi$. This proves the asserted isomorphism.
